analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices with pharmaceutical companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after introduction it was referred to two House committees and its health subcommittee, and no vote was ever scheduled before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since Medicare's drug benefit was created in 2003, a provision in federal law has prohibited the government from negotiating drug prices, leaving Medicare to pay what manufacturers charge. This bill would delete that prohibition and require the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with pharmaceutical manufacturers for drugs covered under the Medicare drug benefit, starting with plan year 2022. The bill was introduced with 12 cosponsors, all Democrats, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 65 million older and disabled Americans, who would pay lower out-of-pocket costs for prescription drugs, and taxpayers, who would pay less toward the Medicare drug benefit if negotiated prices brought down federal spending.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'noninterference' provision (subsection (i) of the Medicare drug benefit statute) that currently bars the government from interfering with the prices manufacturers set, and replaces it with a mandate that the Secretary negotiate prices, discounts, rebates, and other price concessions with drug makers.

The negotiated prices apply to what plans (prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans) may be charged for covered Part D drugs, and nothing prevents individual plans from getting an even lower price below the negotiated one.
Takes effect on enactment and first applies to negotiations and prices for plan years beginning January 1, 2022, so beneficiaries would see the effect quickly rather than after a long phase-in.
Requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations conducted and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public accountability for results.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a government negotiator with Medicare's enormous buying power for the first time and could see lower prices on drugs sold through Medicare's drug benefit.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the Secretary to negotiate but sets no fallback price and no penalty if manufacturers refuse to make concessions, so a company could simply stall, leaving the government without a way to force a deal (the drug-pricing law eventually enacted in 2022 used a stiff excise tax as the enforcement lever).

Pharmaceutical companies argue that lower drug prices reduce revenue available for research and development, which could slow the development of new medicines; the Congressional Budget Office has historically projected significant declines in new-drug introductions from Medicare negotiation proposals (general mechanism; not quantified in the provided sources).
Lower Medicare drug prices shift some cost pressure back onto manufacturers, who could respond by raising prices on new drugs or on drugs sold to people under 65 who lack Medicare's buying power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers is large and immediate: the government would be allowed to use its buying power on behalf of the biggest purchaser of prescription drugs in the world. The main design weakness is that the bill creates a duty to negotiate without a clear enforcement mechanism if manufacturers refuse, so savings could fall short unless the Secretary had real leverage. The industry's R&D argument is genuine but applies to every price-lowering policy, and the 2003 prohibition on negotiation was itself a policy choice, not a natural fact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and their Health Subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 18, 2021 by Rep. Peter Welch with 12 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means, and then to the Health Subcommittee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded on the bill for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

Meanwhile, Congress did enact a narrower version of Medicare drug negotiation in 2022 (the Inflation Reduction Act), which authorized negotiation for a limited set of high-cost drugs starting in 2026 rather than a blanket mandate for all Part D drugs (general knowledge about the 2022 law).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the 2003 statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation in place for the rest of the 117th Congress and continued to set Medicare drug prices without a government negotiator.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 initial supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers for the first time to negotiate prices with the government's largest drug purchaser, ending the 2003 ban on Medicare negotiation. Lower Medicare prices mean lower revenue on Part D drugs, which is why the industry's interest ran against beneficiaries here.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: Plans would pay the lower negotiated prices for covered drugs, and the bill expressly allows plans to bargain for even deeper discounts below the negotiated price. Lower plan drug costs flow through to lower premiums and cost-sharing for beneficiaries.
